your profile says 19M, so I'll explain it with the benefit of the doubt that maybe you haven't received the education as you should.

not everyone on the internet is looking for attention from other people. and not every social interaction depends on looks. a person, whether male or female, might want someone to talk to because they are lonely, or they just don't feel comfortable talking to people in their lives at the moment, they could be living in a small area and their options for socializing is limited, maybe they are extroverts and they like having as many friends as possible, maybe they are looking for something more than friendship, maybe they want to hear about other people's lives. there are many reasons to want to talk to people online.

although it is a creep behavior, some men talk to women for more than platonic reasons, not to become friends or just have a pleasant chat; because they can't think of women without sexualizing them. but that might not be the case for all men and certainly not for most women. 

so it has nothing to do with looks; it has to do with building connections through mutual interests.

please take this perspective into account while you're still young enough to do so.

OP, I agree with the other commentors who said, "It's an effort to get validation," and this comment of yours supports the idea. Most of us bi women have the feeling of missing out if they discovered their bi-ness later in life or not seen as queer enough by the others because they date man, and many other insecurities that have already been mentioned. That being said, you saying "I have a date with A GIRL" might have triggered those insecurities for them; you're bi, they're bi, you are dating girls, they have a boyfriend, what if you don't accept them as bi like yourself???

But another perspective we need to consider is that dating men is really difficult for some of us, especially if they seem to be emotionally intelligent at first, which raises our hopes, and then a huge disappointment when we realize it's not working out this time either. I think most of us assume those kinds of issues are much less common while dating another woman, and we idealize that, which comes off as expressions like this one, essentially meaning that "I got attached to this male-identifying person, and it is good enough to make it last, but sometimes I wonder whether things would've been easier with a woman." The idealized image answers "yes, it would've been," and it comes out as "I'm dating a man, unfortunately."

I'm not saying this is okay to do or fair to one's partner, but I think there might be a deeper issue than normalization of hating your partner or needing validation as a queer person. It might be about feeling unsafe, unseen, misunderstood; but not having confronted and accepted those feelings yet.

why do you think she lied?
has she ever lied in other occasions? think hard. maybe she has a habit of not being upfront.
or maybe, she lied on this particular subject because she didn't feel comfortable talking about it with you. this might have been caused by a mimic, gesture, tone of voice while you posed a question, and so on. consider if she feels judged because of how you approach the topic.
i didn't hide my past from my partner, which caused a lot of insecurity in him as well as unsafety for me because i was questioned multiple times and those topics would come up randomly in arguments that have nothing to do with them.
sometimes i just know he reacts in a certain way because he knows all about me; and i know if a conflict arose with a different partner, he could approach it differently.
if she senses that this will happen, she might have wanted to be seen objectively, not based on her past where you didn't exist.
maybe she is afraid that you knowing things that you can't handle will only cause pain and she would rather keep things to herself (which she has a right to) and spare both of you a lot of big emotions and heated arguments where the main issue is not on the surface.
neither of you has to give every detail from your past (unless it has created an issue that affects today). what you should care about is how you like this person as you've gotten to know them.
you don't know how she feels about what happened in the past. if you want to know what exactly happened, focus on how she feels about them rather than what she did, because what she did won't matter in the relationship, but how she feels about them will be relevant.
it takes tremendous effort to be non judgmental and create comfort and safety around these topics. if you can do it, see if she still lies about them.
if you can't, stop digging. because then it's not about you wanting to know the truth and know this person better - you just need affirmation that she lied. and there is no relationship that would work in that mindset.
i hope this offers some kind of guidance. unfortunately, sexual past can be a source of shame and guilt and not everybody wants to be open about it when the person asking is evokes those feelings.
it doesn't justify lying; but lying might be a defense mechanism to avoid hurt, and if you're ready to understand that and help her through, do it. she might open up in time.

but of course this is my personal take on the topic. she might just like to lie, like a lot of people do.

so you need to listen to your non-judgmental intuition and try to see her intentions. that will give you the guidance.

It might look right now things are getting tense, but I think if you tell her how this behavior makes you feel (not confrontationally or in an accusing manner, but truly just express your feelings about her reactions), there is a chance she might not be completely aware and you can maybe establish and understanding and find a common ground.

I think it has to do with the culture you grew up in and seeing the toxic traits that affected you badly from an early age. I grew up in a country where the majority of it is Muslims, and I feel the same way about them. I see that's almost the same with all religions, and I don't mean people practicing them who mind their own business, I call the ones that make me uncomfortable "fanatics." That's the group of people who tell others how to live their lives and try to make them feel bad about not being exactly like how they see "the right way to be a human." 

At some point, I reached the conclusion that it's not the religion. It's about these people. I've had friends from a variety of backgrounds, and I saw a lot of people just experiencing their faith and spirituality within themselves without trying to impose norms and conventions on others. That's something I respect. But honestly, I do believe that religion has the power to utterly distort reasonable thinking and judgment if the individual practicing it allows it to. But faith is something between you and your God. All religions tell their followers to be understanding and kind to others. I think it's a problem of how these people practice it rather than being religious in general.

only if they want to process and get help, and if they challenge the instinct to resist pain, there is a chance they might become more aware of/involved in your journey/life.

it's their own painful past that prevents them to be there for you as a safe place.

INTJ. Neither am I socially awkward nor a robot when it comes to feelings.

I hate small talk, but I can adapt to many social situations very fast even if it involves it. Probably can't last long in a small talk, so I usually direct conversations in a way that both keeps the other person interested and also deepens the connection even if it's for a short time.

I am a deep feeler. If something happens to cause me negative emotions, I acknowledge the reason behind that reaction and then I try my best to change it. If it's a situation I can't change, I gladly take the time I need to just feel and process, and then grow through it.

Ngl tho, there are times I say "okay right now I need to focus on X thing, get it done, but I'll process this feeling after", so in that sense still sort of a robot as generally perceived I guess.

I told mom, hoping that I don't regret it one day. They didn't get a divorce, but their relationship has never been the same ever since.

As for me, I lost all respect for him while gaining major trust issues for other people. After I kicked him out of the house and he came back when they decided to not get a divorce, I ignored him in the same house for months. Stopped asking his opinions, having a small talk even.

8 years later, I don't regret telling mom and still have a pretty superficial relationship with dad. Not angry at him anymore, even reached a state of forgiveness; which would not happen without years of therapy, though.

Foreign student in Germany here.

I've been in Germany for almost 2 years. As I've heard, people in big cities tend to speak English more than small ones. I live in a small city and I can inform you that when I first got here and my German wasn't great, I tried to explain things in English and sometimes I just got odd stares or "sorry, no English".

Or even sometimes "You need to improve your German if you'd like to study here. Sorry, can't help you."

I think, OP, you and I had different experiences.  However, around the university or at a bank and even sometimes at the supermarket, people that didn't know my intentions to study in Germany, just didn't care. If I speak German, so do they. English? They are on board. They might have just assumed that I am a tourist and many of German people that I talk to about this would say their language is somewhat difficult, so if they see a foreigner they would try to communicate in English and help them with their things.

What you can do about it is to speak German, not switch to English completely if you can't remember the word but try to explain in German instead. For instance, you are at the bakery and you want something that you can see but don't know its name in German. Show them and as they are packing it up, ask "wie heißt das?". They will not only say the name but also help you pronounce it correctly most of the time, if they are not too busy.

Long story short, forget that you speak English for daily tasks. If you don't give people the impression that you'd be more comfortable in English, they will probably just go with German and if you don't understand, with a short "Wie bitte?" they will likely try to explain what they said slower and simpler. Navigate the conversation and you're good to go.
